rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi reads kutub as directives of the sharīʿah, rather than merely books, in this verse.
rows.anchor: This word also means the directives of the shar ī‘ah . Here in this verse, it is used thus.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qayyimah means straight, clear, and explicit; the people wanted explicit religious directives and resisted unrelated material.
rows.anchor: means “straight, clear and explicit.” In other words, they desired explicit directives

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their demand for written sheets matching the stone tablets of the Torah is presented with biting ridicule.
rows.anchor: their demand was that just as the ten commandments of the Torah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān answers the demand, which the People of the Book planted among Quraysh: even a demanded miracle would not make these people believe.
rows.anchor: even if these people are shown a miracle on their demand, they are not ones who would believe.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their history shows that God gave them the law alongside extraordinary signs, including the tablets, Sinai raised above them, and water from the mountain.
rows.anchor: whatever shar ī‘ah they were given, was given in the company of some open miracles.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Despite these signs, they worshipped Samiri’s calf; this began their great dissension, which grew until difference was all they shared.
rows.anchor: the manner in which they fulfilled their covenant with the shar ī‘ah was that they started worshipping a calf fashioned out by S āmar ī.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their dissension left no fundamental religious tenet to which they adhered; they disagreed across religion and lost many teachings through this attitude.
rows.anchor: there was not a single fundamental tenet of religion to which they adhered. They had serious differences in every tenet of religion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They abandoned exclusive monotheism, worshipping the calf, treating ʿUzayr as God's son and scholars as partners, and practicing sorcery and idolatry.
rows.anchor: their prophet, they worshipped the calf, deemed ‘Uzayr

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They were also commanded to pray, but prayer was neglected so thoroughly that the Torah no longer mentions it, although it describes animal sacrifice.
rows.anchor: they totally disregarded the prayer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zakāh remained formally present, but Levite scholars rather than the poor became its real recipients; scripture depicts those scholars' greed.
rows.anchor: instead of the poor and needy, the religious scholars of the Levites became

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The declaration that this is the religion of the upright nation answers the earlier demand for clear written directives.
rows.anchor: are actually an answer to their demand mentioned earlier by the words

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The implication is that Abraham's natural, upright religious directives were already explicit, and the Qurʾān likewise states clear directives; their objections arise from jealousy and a wish to deprive others of God's law.
rows.anchor: they had already been given them in the capacity of the upright and very natural directives of the religion of Abraham

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Classical Arabic suppresses the noun qualified by al-qayyimah when context signals it; the implied phrase is the religion of the upright millah.
rows.anchor: which is customary in classical Arabic

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These basic teachings passed to both branches of Abraham's family as an inheritance from their forefather, making opposition to them especially lamentable.
rows.anchor: these are the basic directives of religion which were transferred to both branches of the family of Abraham

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān calls Abraham's nation a millah qayyimah and cites 6:161 for the natural religion of Abraham joined with complete devotion.
rows.anchor: Say: “My Lord has guided me to a straight path: the natural religion of the nation of Abraham, with complete devotion.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse describes the fate of rejecting People of the Book and idolaters and condemns their conceit and pride as causes of rejection.
rows.anchor: the fate of people whether from the People of the Book or from the Idolaters who were adamant in rejecting the Qur’ ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Book recipients receive no lenience if they become blind to truth like idolaters; Hell is their eternal abode, against their claim that its fire would touch them briefly or not at all.
rows.anchor: It is also emphasized that Hell shall be their eternal

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling them the worst creatures rebukes leaders who demand angels or open scriptures and refuse a prophet of lower worldly status; truth from God requires submission, while rejecting it aligns one with Satan's progeny.
rows.anchor: As per this pride, they were not willing to obey and accept someone as a prophet of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers preserved respect for truth, accepted God's Book, and did righteous deeds without the conceited demand made by the rejecters, so the Qurʾān calls them the best creatures.
rows.anchor: they professed faith in the Book of God and did righteous deeds. The Qur’ ān has said that such people are the best of creatures.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human worth rests on intellectual and moral ability rather than wealth, resources, family, or lineage: believing Roman and Abyssinian slaves outrank Quraysh and Hashimite leaders lacking those qualities.
rows.anchor: the real value of a person is not on the basis of his wealth and resources, family and lineage but on the basis of his intellectual and moral abilities.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humans are created in the best mould and can become God's best creatures by recognizing their worth, but indifference can reduce them to the lowest; their ascent and descent have no limit, hence the sages' counsel to know oneself.
rows.anchor: The Almighty has created him in the best of moulds with great abilities.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The best of God’s creatures, despite the trials of this life, receive eternal gardens beneath which rivers flow.
rows.anchor: Mentioned in this verse is the reward of those who are the best of God’s creatures.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is pleased because they fulfilled worship and service as commanded; they are pleased because He kept His promises and gave beyond their hopes.
rows.anchor: they fulfilled their obligation of

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reward is for those who trust prophetic reports about unseen realities using reason rather than waiting to see everything; success merits God's favor, while failure leaves one worse than an animal and unworthy of blessing.
rows.anchor: In this world, the real trial of a person is that while

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah depicts the coming day when every deed, including hidden acts, is exposed and repaid, with each person answerable alone and without help or intercession.
rows.anchor: every deed done by man is brought to light is depicted. All his labours will be exposed and nothing will remain hidden.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cataclysm casts out what is buried; at God's intimation earth recounts human deeds, after which every person sees even the smallest good and evil.
rows.anchor: The earth will then narrate its story at the intimation of the Almighty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah answers three denial-based misconceptions: doubt that the world will end, doubt that every person's deeds can be counted, and belief that associated deities can intercede and secure rank.
rows.anchor: Firstly, they had extreme doubts about the destruction of this world.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Idhā in this construction recalls or warns the hearer to keep the coming time in mind.
rows.anchor: serves as a reminder of what

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zilzāl is an emphatic absolute object, and its annexation to earth adds a nuance: it will shake as destined, with an unimaginable but certain force, so people should stay alert.
rows.anchor: the correct meaning is: “when the earth shall be shaken the way it ought to be shaken”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thiqal means weight or burden, primarily the dead cast out at resurrection, and more generally buried treasure and concealed crimes; Islahi refers also to 84:4 and 100:9.
rows.anchor: its foremost connotation are the dead who have been buried in the earth and who will be thrown overboard by it on the Day of Judgement.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cry describes people's consternation at the earth's continuing convulsion and expulsion of its contents; evildoers will likewise be shaken on seeing their records, as 49:18 says no deed escapes the strange Book.
rows.anchor: Struck with consternation they will cry out:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earth recounts good and evil deeds; elsewhere the Qurʾān says criminals' limbs, skins, and hairs will speak and testify against them.
rows.anchor: the limbs of criminals will be given the power of speech by the Almighty on the Day of Judgement.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because human acts occur on or beneath earth, it is the greatest witness; God gives it speech just as He gives speech to human organs, and 41:21 describes the same divine enabling.
rows.anchor: the earth also will be made vocal by Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word wa means intimation or indication: earth speaks only at God's command, and 84:5 likewise says it obeys its Lord's directive.
rows.anchor: The implication is that the earth will rehearse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ashtāt means separately or singly: people emerge without family, tribe, companions, wealth, supporters, or intercessors, as also stated in 19:95 and 6:94.
rows.anchor: means “in a separate or solitary manner.” In other words

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about deeds being shown gives the reason people are brought before God: they experience the results of their worldly labours; the verb “shown” denotes its outcome.
rows.anchor: express the reason why people will be brought before the Almighty.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Everyone sees good and evil deeds, but under a Qurʾānic principle some believers' sins are compensated by good deeds, while some disbelievers' good deeds earn no reward because misdeeds and heretical beliefs nullify them.
rows.anchor: a believer may not see some of his evil deeds because some of the good ones will have compensated for them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After judgment by this principle, eternal bliss or ruin follows according to the balance of deeds in 101:6–9.
rows.anchor: Hence, whose scales are heavy will dwell in bliss, and whose scales are light, the abyss of Hell will be his abode.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūrah al-ʿĀdiyāt rebukes human ingratitude: people obtain their means through God's gifts yet neglect their obligations and turn God-given abilities against Him, heedless of the day secrets will be exposed and judged.
rows.anchor: man has been warned and rebuked for being ungrateful.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Its subject matches the previous sūrah, al-Zilzāl, but al-Zilzāl portrays the Day of Judgment while al-ʿĀdiyāt explains the cause for its coming.
rows.anchor: the first portrays the day when all this will happen and the second cites the reason which entails the coming of that day

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sequence uses war horses' obedience, bravery, diligence, and sacrifice to rebuke people who ignore their duty to serve God; it ends by exposing greed and warning that earthly possessions and heart-secrets will be revealed, so the wise prepare.
rows.anchor: the bravery, diligence and sacrifices displayed by war horses in obedience and love for their masters are initially cited as evidence.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ʿādiyāt means running and describes war horses, since the four following adjectives suit them; the camels of Muzdalifah interpretation has no corroboration and does not fit those adjectives.
rows.anchor: means “to run.” Here it is mentioned as an adjective

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alternative that the word means warriors' horses is unsupported, especially because it leaves the oath unrelated to verse 6's assertion that man is ungrateful to God.
rows.anchor: What relationship can these words of the muqsam ‘alayh have with the horses of the warriors and the combatants?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both alternative readings wrongly assume that oath objects must be sacred; Islahi rejects that assumption and says the real point is their testimony.
rows.anchor: Both these interpretations are based on the false notion that it is essential that things which are sworn by should be sacred.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūrahs al-Fīl and Quraysh warn Quraysh that security and sustenance came through Abraham's prayer and the House's blessing, not their own merit; they must worship the Lord who fed and secured them, as 106:3–4 says.
rows.anchor: they have been blessed with peace and sustenance not because of their own efforts or because they were entitled to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Fīl recounts an event demonstrating God's power in saving the House from an enemy, whereas Quraysh attributes peace and sustenance to their association with the House.
rows.anchor: The only difference between the two sūrahs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham prayed for peace and sustenance after settling Ishmael in a food-scarce, conflict-ridden Makkah; the family benefited through the House, then became proud and ungrateful; al-Balad also treats this attitude.
rows.anchor: Abraham (sws) had earnestly prayed to the Almighty to bless the land with peace and sustenance and the Almighty had granted him his wish.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God decisively aided Quraysh against Abrahah's sixty-thousand-strong force attacking the House; they could not face it openly and withdrew toward the mountains.
rows.anchor: The Almighty had helped them decidedly

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The invading army's vanguard had elephants; Quraysh's frail defense from nearby mountains was transformed by God into the enemy's destruction, after which birds fed on their bodies.
rows.anchor: dead bodies were feasted u pon

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although al-am tara is grammatically singular, Qurʾānic usage commonly addresses a group by addressing each person; here Quraysh are addressed about a recent event many had witnessed or widely heard of.
rows.anchor: they are reminded about their recent past and asked whether they had forgotten how their Lord had dealt with the People of the Elephant.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The event occurred in the Prophet's birth year, and its direct witnesses or widely repeated reports make the wording “Have you not seen?” apt.
rows.anchor: had taken place the same year

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān omits the attackers' details because its audience knew them; “People of the Elephant” identifies Abrahah, the Abyssinian Yemen ruler, whose army used elephants, and recalls Arabs' first encounter with them in war.
rows.anchor: The reason for this brevity is that the addressed people knew these details very well.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording leaves open whether the army had one elephant or several.
rows.anchor: Whether there was only a single elephant or several,

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Against historians who call Abrahah tolerant, Islahi depicts him as an opportunistic, treacherous, prejudiced Christian who seized Yemen, killed its Jewish ruler, and persecuted Judaism.
rows.anchor: a traitor and highly prejudiced Christian.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abrahah sought conversion of Arabs by building a cathedral in Ṣanʿāʾ and told Negus he would divert pilgrimage there and demolish the Baytullāh.
rows.anchor: converting the Arabs to Christianity.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi calls the claim that an Arab defiled the cathedral a contrived pretext: Arab bravery makes it unlikely, and even if true an individual's act cannot justify punishing a nation or razing the House.
rows.anchor: a person’s individual misdeed is not enough

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abrahah attacked Makkah with sixty thousand troops and nine or ten elephants.
rows.anchor: with a sixty thousand army supported by nine or ten

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān calls the plan an intrigue because Abrahah invented a ridiculous allegation to justify a vicious attack.
rows.anchor: The Almighty aborted the scheme of Abrahah

rows.speaker: Imam Farāhī
rows.claim: Farāhī lists three ways the attack was contrived: it came in forbidden months, during the Hajj rites, and at Minā when pilgrims sacrificed or were exhausted on their return.
rows.anchor: Imam Far āhī mentions them in his exegesis:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the wording could allow one elephant or several, Islahi prefers multiple elephants because the term is plural and hadith reports describe a battery of them.
rows.anchor: there was a whole battery of elephants

rows.speaker: Imam Farāhī
rows.claim: Farāhī explains that God foiled Abrahah by stopping the army at Wādī Muḥaṣṣar, enabling Arabs to use its stones, and sending a destructive stone-hurling wind.
rows.anchor: He did not let them penetrate beyond

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Eyewitnesses reported the ḥāṣib wind, historians including Ibn Hishām recorded testimony, and Farāhī discusses it at length.
rows.anchor: Many eye witnesses have reported this

rows.speaker: Abū Qays
rows.claim: The poet Abū Qays invokes the ḥāṣib as a sign of divine power, saying it wrapped the attackers like rubbish.
rows.anchor: The famous poet Ab ū Qays while mentioning the power and glory of the Almighty refers to this ḥāṣib

rows.speaker: Ṣayfī ibn ʿĀmir
rows.claim: Ṣayfī ibn ʿĀmir refers to both a ḥāṣib and a ṣayf, with the latter described as similar but differing in intensity.
rows.anchor: Ṣayf ī ibn ‘ Āmir has referred to a ḥāṣib
